title: New Hollywood
wiki_lead:
The New Hollywood, Hollywood Renaissance, or American New Wave, was a movement in American film history from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s, when a new generation of filmmakers came to prominence. They influenced the types of film produced, their production and marketing, and the way major studios approached filmmaking.
It was precipitated by the demise of the studio system and the rise of television, after which the commercial success of films was diminished. In New Hollywood films, the film director, rather than the studio, took on a key authorial role.
The definition of "New Hollywood" varies, depending on the author, with some defining it as a movement and others as a period. The span of the period is also a subject of debate, as well as its integrity, as some authors, such as Thomas Schatz, argue that the New Hollywood consists of several different movements. The films made in this movement are stylistically characterized in that their narrative often deviated from classical norms. 
Successful films of the early New Hollywood era include Bonnie and Clyde, The Graduate, and Easy Rider while films whose box office failure marked the end of the era include New York, New York, Sorcerer, Heaven's Gate, They All Laughed, and One from the Heart.

History


Background

Following the Paramount Case (which ended block booking and ownership of theater chains by film studios) and the advent of television (where Gore Vidal, Rod Serling, John Frankenheimer, Arthur Penn, Paddy Chayefsky and Sidney Lumet worked in their earlier years), both of which severely weakened both the traditional studio system and the Motion Picture Production Code (or the Hays Code), Hollywood studios initially used spectacle to retain profitability. Technicolor developed a far more widespread use, while widescreen processes and technical improvements, such as CinemaScope, stereo sound, and others, such as 3-D, were invented to retain the dwindling audience and compete with television. However, these were generally unsuccessful in increasing profits. By 1957, Life magazine called the 1950s "the horrible decade" for Hollywood. It was dubbed a "New Hollywood" by a press.
In the 1950s and early 1960s, Hollywood was dominated by musicals, historical epics, and other films that benefited from the larger screens, wider framing, and improved sound. However, audience shares continued to dwindle, and had reached alarmingly low levels by the mid-1960s. Several costly flops, including Doctor Dolittle, Tora! Tora! Tora! and the Julie Andrews vehicle Star!, each failed attempts to replicate the success of Mary Poppins, Doctor Zhivago and The Sound of Music, put great strain on the studios. Both British and American press dismissed filmmakers Alfred Hitchcock and Howard Hawks as "frivolous entertainers and nothing more" while praising more respectable "models of American art films" like Stanley Kramer's Judgment at Nuremberg. grok_lead: New Hollywood, also referred to as the American New Wave or Hollywood Renaissance, was a transformative period in American cinema spanning roughly from 1967 to the early 1980s, during which young, often film school-trained directors gained unprecedented creative control, leading to innovative storytelling, stylistic experimentation, and explorations of morally complex characters amid social and political turmoil. This era emerged from the weakening of the traditional studio system, exacerbated by the 1948 Paramount Decree that dismantled vertical integration, competition from television, and costly flops of spectacle films like musicals in the 1960s, prompting studios to take risks on independent-minded filmmakers to appeal to a youth-dominated audience comprising about 80% of moviegoers aged 16-25. The abandonment of the Hays Code in 1968, replaced by the MPAA ratings system, removed longstanding censorship barriers on depictions of sex, violence, and profanity, enabling films with explicit content and anti-establishment themes influenced by European New Waves and countercultural movements like the Vietnam War protests and civil rights struggles. Pioneering works such as Bonnie and Clyde (1967) and The Graduate (1967) shattered box office expectations while challenging conventions, followed by landmark achievements including The Godfather (1972), which earned critical acclaim and commercial success, and Taxi Driver (1976), exemplifying gritty urban realism and psychological depth under directors like Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, and Robert Altman. Though celebrated for elevating directors as auteurs and producing enduring classics, the movement faced controversies over graphic violence and sympathetic portrayals of outlaws or anti-heroes, and its decline accelerated with budget overruns in films like Heaven's Gate (1980), shifting Hollywood toward safer blockbuster formulas epitomized by Jaws (1975) and Star Wars (1977).
